claims.statement_id: Seorang lelaki dari jauh berkata Perchta tak dapat dipercaya karena Heimchen arwah anak belum dibaptis; ketika warga menjauhi Heimchen, Perchta dan Heimchen menyeberangi sungai dan tak kembali.
claims.quote: One day, though, a serious man came from afar who told the people that Perchta isn't to be trusted as the Heimchen are the souls of unbaptized children. When the people then avoided the Heimchen, Perchta decided that it was time to leave, and she and the Heimchen crossed the stream never to return again.

claims.statement: In folk belief (Volksglauben) the cricket (Grille) in the house was held to be a bringer of luck (Glücksbringer).
claims.statement_id: Dalam kepercayaan rakyat (Volksglauben), jangkrik (Grille) di dalam rumah dianggap pembawa keberuntungan (Glücksbringer).
claims.quote: Im Volksglauben galt die Grille im Haus als Glücksbringer.

claims.statement: The Heimchen (Acheta domesticus), also called Hausgrille, is an insect of the true cricket family (Gryllidae).
claims.statement_id: Heimchen (Acheta domesticus), juga disebut Hausgrille, adalah serangga dari famili jangkrik sejati (Gryllidae).
claims.quote: Das Heimchen (Acheta domesticus), auch Hausgrille, ist eine Langfühlerschrecke aus der Familie der Echten Grillen (Gryllidae).

description.en: Hemaraja (Thai: เหมราช) is a creature found in Thai and possibly South Asian mythology. It is said to be the combination of a hema (an ill-defined creature in and of itself; usually likened to a swan but sometimes depicted more like a crocodile) and a lion.

claims.statement: The hemaraja (เหมราช) is a creature of Thai and possibly South Asian mythology.
claims.statement_id: Hemaraja (เหมราช) adalah makhluk dalam mitologi Thai dan mungkin Asia Selatan.
claims.quote: Hemaraja (Thai: เหมราช) is a creature found in Thai and possibly South Asian mythology.

claims.statement: It is said to combine a hema (an ill-defined creature, usually swan-like but sometimes more like a crocodile) and a lion.
claims.statement_id: Hemaraja dikatakan gabungan hema (makhluk yang kurang jelas, biasanya disamakan dengan angsa tetapi kadang lebih mirip buaya) dan singa.
claims.quote: It is said to be the combination of a hema (an ill-defined creature in and of itself; usually likened to a swan but sometimes depicted more like a crocodile) and a lion.

description.en: In English folklore, Herne the Hunter is a ghost associated with Windsor Forest and Great Park in the English county of Berkshire. He is said to have antlers growing from his head, ride a horse, torment cattle, and rattle chains. The earliest mention of Herne comes from William Shakespeare's 1597 play The Merry Wives of Windsor, and it is impossible to know how accurately or to what degree Shakespeare may have incorporated a real local legend into his work, though there have been several later attempts to connect Herne to historical figures, pagan deities, or ancient archetypes.

claims.statement: In English folklore Herne the Hunter is a ghost of Windsor Forest and Great Park in Berkshire, antlered, horse-riding, tormenting cattle and rattling chains.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita rakyat Inggris (English folklore), Herne the Hunter adalah hantu Windsor Forest dan Great Park di Berkshire, bertanduk rusa, menunggang kuda, menyiksa ternak, dan menggemerincingkan rantai.
claims.quote: In English folklore, Herne the Hunter is a ghost associated with Windsor Forest and Great Park in the English county of Berkshire. He is said to have antlers growing from his head, ride a horse, torment cattle, and rattle chains.

claims.statement: Herne is first mentioned in William Shakespeare's 1597 play The Merry Wives of Windsor; how far it used a real local legend is unknown.
claims.statement_id: Sebutan tertua Herne dari lakon William Shakespeare The Merry Wives of Windsor (1597); tak diketahui seberapa jauh ia memakai legenda setempat.
claims.quote: The earliest mention of Herne comes from William Shakespeare's 1597 play The Merry Wives of Windsor, and it is impossible to know how accurately or to what degree Shakespeare may have incorporated a real local legend into his work

claims.statement: Shakespeare: all winter at midnight Herne walks round an oak with great ragged horns, blasts the tree, makes milch-kine yield blood and shakes a chain.
claims.statement_id: Shakespeare: sepanjang musim dingin, tengah malam, Herne mengelilingi pohon ek dengan tanduk besar, merusak pohon, membuat sapi perah (milch-kine) mengeluarkan darah, dan menggemerincingkan rantai.
claims.quote: Doth all the winter-time, at still midnight Walk round about an oak, with great ragg'd horns; And there he blasts the tree, and takes the cattle, And makes milch-kine yield blood, and shakes a chain In a most hideous and dreadful manner.

claims.statement: The 1602 first quarto says the ghost, Horne, was invented to scare children into obedience, walking the forest as a great stag.
claims.statement_id: Kuarto pertama (1602) menyebut hantu Horne diciptakan untuk menakuti anak-anak agar patuh, berwujud rusa jantan besar.
claims.quote: The first quarto of the play from 1602 includes a different version of this text, which states that the ghost (spelled "Horne" in this version) was invented to scare children into obedience, and that mothers tell their children the tale of a ghost who walks the forest in the form of a great stag.

claims.statement: Official versions call Herne the ghost of a former Windsor Forest keeper haunting an oak at midnight in winter.
claims.statement_id: Versi resmi lakon menyebut Herne arwah bekas penjaga Windsor Forest yang menghantui pohon ek pada tengah malam di musim dingin.
claims.quote: Officially published versions of the play refer only to the tale of Herne as the ghost of a former Windsor Forest keeper who haunts a particular oak tree at midnight in the winter time.

claims.statement: Herne is read as a god of the hunt (Gott der Jagd) and lord of game (Herr des Wildes), perhaps a local Anglo-Saxon (Angelsachsen) god of Windsor Forest; some equate him with Cernunnos.
claims.statement_id: Herne ditafsirkan sebagai dewa perburuan (Gott der Jagd) dan penguasa satwa (Herr des Wildes), mungkin dewa lokal Anglo-Saxon (Angelsachsen) di Windsor Forest; ada yang menyamakannya dengan Cernunnos.
claims.quote: Herne wird als Gott der Jagd und Herr des Wildes gedeutet. Vermutungen zufolge war Herne eine Lokalgottheit der Angelsachsen im Windsor Forest, einem Wald, der sich über die heutigen Grafschaften Berkshire, Buckinghamshire und Hampshire erstreckte. Man nimmt an, Herne sei identisch mit Cernunnos

claims.statement: Others see Herne as a form of the Germanic god (germanischen Gottes) Odin in the Wild Hunt (Wilden Jagd).
claims.statement_id: Sebaliknya, ada yang melihat Herne sebagai wujud dewa Jermanik (germanischen Gottes) Odin dalam Perburuan Liar (Wilden Jagd).
claims.quote: Konträr dazu sieht man in Herne eine Erscheinungsform des germanischen Gottes Odin bei der Wilden Jagd.

description.en: A Hingchabi (Meitei: ꯍꯤꯡꯆꯥꯕꯤ, Old Manipuri: ꯍꯤꯡꯆꯥꯄꯤ, romanized: hing-chaa-pee, lit. 'giantess') is a mythical creature in Meitei mythology, folklore and religion (Sanamahism) of Antique Kangleipak (Ancient Manipur). She has characters similar to those of the vampires as well as the witches. The terms, "hing" means "raw" and "chaa" means "to eat" in Meitei language (Manipuri language).

claims.statement: Hingchabi is a creature of Meitei mythology, folklore and religion in Kangleipak.
claims.statement_id: Hingchabi adalah makhluk dalam mitologi, cerita rakyat, dan agama Meitei di Kangleipak.
claims.quote:
A Hingchabi (Meitei: ꯍꯤꯡꯆꯥꯕꯤ, Old Manipuri: ꯍꯤꯡꯆꯥꯄꯤ, romanized: hing-chaa-pee, lit. 'giantess') is a mythical creature in Meitei mythology, folklore and religion (Sanamahism) of Antique Kangleipak (Ancient Manipur). She has characters similar to those of the vampires as well as the witches.
The terms, "hing" means "raw" and "chaa" means "to eat" in Meitei language (Manipuri language).

description.en: Hito-gitsune or ninko (人狐) is a type of spirit possession told about in legends of the Chūgoku region of western Japan.

claims.statement: Hito-gitsune are possessing spirits in traditions of western Japan’s Chūgoku region.
claims.statement_id: Hito-gitsune adalah roh perasuk dalam tradisi wilayah Chūgoku di Jepang barat.
claims.quote: Hito-gitsune or ninko (人狐) is a type of spirit possession told about in legends of the Chūgoku region of western Japan.

claims.statement: The spirit is described as martenlike, with possession bringing illness and mental disturbance.
claims.statement_id: Roh digambarkan mirip marten, dengan kerasukan membawa penyakit dan gangguan pikiran.
claims.quote: They are said to be the spirit of a Japanese marten-like animal, and it is said that those possessed by one would be afflicted with stomach aches and mental abnormalities.

claims.statement: A regional variant identifies it with a pond-dwelling water weasel.
claims.statement_id: Varian daerah mengidentifikasikannya dengan cerpelai air penghuni kolam.
claims.quote: In some areas, it is said that a mizu-itachi (水鼬, water weasel) within ponds are hito-gitsune.

claims.statement: Families may gain wealth through it, but mistreatment is said to reverse their fortunes.
claims.statement_id: Keluarga dapat memperoleh kekayaan melaluinya, tetapi perlakuan buruk disebut membalikkan nasib mereka.
claims.quote: Also, families that have hito-gitsune would grow wealthy as a result of the hito-gitsune carrying back riches, but if someone of the family mistreats the hito-gitsune, the fortunes of the family, no matter how rich they were, would immediately decline.

claims.statement: Hearn describes a weasel-sized body with a fox’s tail.
claims.statement_id: Hearn menggambarkan tubuh seukuran cerpelai dengan ekor rubah.
claims.quote: It is no larger than a weasel, and somewhat similar in shape, except for its tail, which is like the tail of any other fox.

claims.statement: It stays invisible to people other than those it attaches to.
claims.statement_id: Ia tetap tidak terlihat oleh orang selain mereka yang ditempelinya.
claims.quote: It is rarely seen, keeping itself invisible, except to those to whom it attaches itself.

description.en: Hồ ly tinh (chữ Hán: 狐狸精) also known as Hồ tiên (狐仙), Hồ ly (狐狸), Hồ tinh (狐精), Hồ yêu (狐妖), Yêu hồ (妖狐) or Cáo chín đuôi (chữ Nôm: 𤞺𠃩𡳪), Cáo tinh (𤞺精) is a nine-tailed fox in Vietnamese mythology. They do not have a specific personality; some stories tell about them harming people but along with them are stories about them helping people. According to a quite famous version, hồ ly tinh are foxes that have the ability to cultivate, to be able to transform, and have magic. If they practice for a hundred years, then they will have three tails and are called Yêu hồ or Tam vĩ yêu hồ (Three-tails demon fox). If they cultivate until after 1,000 years, they change to Lục vĩ ma hồ (Six-tailed ghost fox). And so, when they reach the realm of 9-tails, Cửu vĩ hồ (九尾狐) or Cửu vĩ thiên hồ (Nine-tailed celestial fox), they can turn into humans. Each tail is a life of them. To kill a fox, you must cut off its tail first.

claims.statement: The hồ ly tinh (狐狸精), also hồ tiên, hồ ly or cáo chín đuôi, is a nine-tailed fox of Vietnamese mythology; it has no fixed personality, with stories of foxes harming and helping people.
claims.statement_id: Hồ ly tinh (狐狸精), juga hồ tiên, hồ ly, atau cáo chín đuôi, adalah rubah berekor sembilan dalam mitologi Vietnam; sifatnya tidak tetap, ada kisah rubah yang mencelakai dan ada yang menolong orang.
claims.quote: is a nine-tailed fox in Vietnamese mythology. They do not have a specific personality; some stories tell about them harming people but along with them are stories about them helping people.

claims.statement: In a famous version, hồ ly tinh are foxes that can cultivate, transform and work magic; after a hundred years three tails, after a thousand six, and at nine (cửu vĩ hồ) they can become human; each tail is a life, and to kill one its tails must first be cut.
claims.statement_id: Menurut versi terkenal, hồ ly tinh adalah rubah yang dapat berlatih, berubah wujud, dan bersihir; setelah seratus tahun berekor tiga, setelah seribu tahun berekor enam, dan saat berekor sembilan (cửu vĩ hồ) dapat menjelma manusia; tiap ekor satu nyawa, dan untuk membunuhnya ekornya harus dipotong dulu.
claims.quote: According to a quite famous version, hồ ly tinh are foxes that have the ability to cultivate, to be able to transform, and have magic. If they practice for a hundred years, then they will have three tails

claims.statement: In the Lĩnh Nam chích quái, the hồ ly tinh harms good people and is killed by Lạc Long Quân; a white nine-tailed fox in a cave took the form of a handsome man or beautiful girl to lure young people.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kitab Lĩnh Nam chích quái, hồ ly tinh digambarkan sebagai binatang yang mencelakai orang baik lalu dibunuh Lạc Long Quân; rubah putih berekor sembilan di sebuah gua menjelma laki-laki atau perempuan rupawan untuk memikat pemuda-pemudi.
claims.quote: In the book Lĩnh Nam chích quái, the Hồ ly tinh (or Hồ tinh) is also mentioned with the image of an animal that causes harm to good people, then is killed by Lạc Long Quân to eliminate harm to the people.

claims.statement: After Lạc Long Quân attacked the cave with water, the place became a deep pool called Xác Cáo lagoon, today's Tây Hồ.
claims.statement_id: Setelah Lạc Long Quân menyerang gua itu dengan air, tempat itu menjadi kolam dalam bernama laguna Xác Cáo, yang kini Tây Hồ.
claims.quote: This place became a deep pool called Xác Cáo lagoon (Fox Corpses lagoon), which is Tây Hồ today.

claims.statement: West Lake is the tomb where the nine-tailed fox is buried.
claims.statement_id: Danau Barat adalah makam tempat rubah berekor sembilan dikuburkan.
claims.quote: West Lake is the tomb where the nine-tailed fox is buried.

description.en: Hödekin (variously spelled Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin, and Hütchen, etc.) is a kobold (house spirit) of German folklore. The name, a diminutive meaning "Little Hat", refers to the pileus hat he wears, a style which was common in Ancient Greece and later various parts of Europe. Hödekin is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernard (Bernhardus), Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim, located in Lower Saxony. In some versions of the legend, the spirit inhabits Winzenburg, a county which he helped the bishopric obtain. Though Hödekin did not initiate harm, he was murderously vindictive. He dismembered a kitchen boy after the boy habitually insulted him and poured kitchen filth upon him. When the cook (who hadn't controlled the misbehaving boy) griped, the sprite tainted the meat for the bishop with toad blood and venom. When the cook remained unfazed, Hödekin pushed him into a ditch from a great height, killing him. Hödekin's actions weren't always malicious. He once helped a man by fiercely protecting his wife. When the man jokingly entrusted his wife to Hödekin during his absence, the sprite took it seriously and chased off every man who called on the adulterous wife. He also helped an idiot clerk appointed to the synod by giving him a ring made of laurel leaves that granted him knowledge and intelligence. Ultimately, the spirit's time in Hildesheim ended when the bishop exorcised him with ecclesiastical incantations and drove him out of the city.

claims.statement: Hödekin (also Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin and Hütchen) is a kobold (house spirit) of German folklore; the name, a diminutive meaning 'Little Hat', refers to the pileus cap he wears.
claims.statement_id: Hödekin (juga Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin, dan Hütchen) adalah kobold (roh rumah) dalam cerita rakyat Jerman; namanya bentuk kecil yang berarti "Topi Kecil", merujuk topi pileus yang dikenakannya.
claims.quote: Hödekin (variously spelled Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin , and Hütchen , etc.) is a kobold (house spirit) of German folklore. The name, a diminutive meaning "Little Hat", refers to the pileus hat he wears

claims.quote: Hödekin is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernard (Bernhardus), Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim, located in Lower Saxony. In some versions of the legend, the spirit inhabits Winzenburg, a county which he helped the bishopric obtain.

claims.statement_id: Meski tidak memulai kejahatan, Hödekin pendendam yang mematikan: ia memotong-motong bocah dapur yang terus menghina dan menuangkan kotoran kepadanya, meracuni daging uskup dengan darah dan bisa kodok saat juru masak mengeluh, lalu mendorong juru masak ke parit dari ketinggian hingga tewas.
claims.quote: Though Hödekin did not initiate harm, he was murderously vindictive. He dismembered a kitchen boy after the boy habitually insulted him and poured kitchen filth upon him. When the cook ... griped, the sprite tainted the meat for the bishop with toad blood and venom. When the cook remained unfazed, Hödekin pushed him into a ditch from a great height, killing him.

claims.statement: Hödeken is the castle spirit of Winzenburg, a dwarf-like figure (kobold) who also carried messages between Hildesheim and Winzenburg; the road between Winzenburg and Hildesheim's Domhof that he reputedly ran to report the last count of Winzenburg's death is called the 'Rennstieg'.
claims.statement_id: Hödeken adalah roh kastel Winzenburg, sosok mirip kurcaci (kobold) yang juga menjadi pembawa pesan antara Hildesheim dan Winzenburg; jalan antara Winzenburg dan Domhof Hildesheim yang konon dilaluinya untuk mengabarkan kematian Graf Winzenburg terakhir disebut "Rennstieg".
claims.quote: Der Hödeken ist der Burggeist der Winzenburg. Er wird als eine zwergenartige Gestalt beschrieben (Kobold), die auch als Bote zwischen Hildesheim und Winzenburg Nachrichten übermittelte. Der Weg zwischen Winzenburg und Hildesheimer Domhof, den Hödeken nach dem Tod des letzten Grafen von Winzenburg entlanggeeilt sein soll, um die Todesnachricht zu überbringen, wird „Rennstieg“ genannt.

claims.statement: Per the Brothers Grimm, Hödeken was a spirit at the court of the Bishop of Hildesheim who kept the night watch awake, gave the bishop military advice, warned him of dangers, sometimes helped other townsfolk, and was once asked to guard a man's wife in his absence.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Grimm bersaudara, Hödeken adalah roh di istana Uskup Hildesheim yang mencegah penjaga malam tertidur, memberi uskup nasihat perang, memperingatkannya akan bahaya, kadang menolong warga Hildesheim lain, dan pernah diminta menjaga istri seseorang selama suaminya pergi.
claims.quote: Der Hödeken war ein Geist, der sich am Hof des Bischofs von Hildesheim aufhielt. Er hinderte die Nachtwachen am Einschlafen, gab dem Bischof militärische Ratschläge und warnte ihn vor kommenden Gefahren. Gelegentlich half er auch anderen Hildesheimern. Einmal bat jemand den Hödeken, seine Frau während seiner Abwesenheit zu beschützen.

claims.statement: He also helped a foolish clerk appointed to the synod with a ring of laurel leaves granting knowledge and intelligence; his time in Hildesheim ended when the bishop exorcised him with ecclesiastical incantations and drove him out.
claims.statement_id: Ia juga menolong seorang juru tulis bodoh yang diangkat ke sinode dengan memberinya cincin daun salam yang memberi pengetahuan dan kecerdasan; akhirnya masa tinggalnya di Hildesheim berakhir ketika uskup mengusirnya dengan mantra gerejawi.
claims.quote: He also helped an idiot clerk appointed to the synod by giving him a ring made of laurel leaves that granted him knowledge and intelligence. Ultimately, the spirit's time in Hildesheim ended when the bishop exorcised him with ecclesiastical incantations and drove him out of the city.

claims.statement: When the man returned, Hödeken complained he would rather herd all the pigs of Saxony than guard such a woman again.
claims.statement_id: Ketika lelaki itu kembali, Hödeken mengeluh bahwa ia lebih suka menggembala semua babi di Sachsen daripada menjaga perempuan seperti itu lagi.
claims.quote: Als der Mann zurückkehrte, beschwerte sich der Hödeken: Er werde lieber alle Schweine von Sachsen hüten als nochmals eine solche Frau.

claims.statement: Per the Grimms, he wore a little felt hat, whence the name Hütchen, in Low Saxon Hödeken.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Grimm bersaudara, ia memakai topi laken kecil di kepalanya, sehingga diberi nama Hütchen, dalam bahasa Saxon Rendah Hödeken.
claims.quote: „[…] auf dem Haupt trug er einen kleinen Filzhut, wovon man ihm den Namen Hütchen auf Niedersächsisch Hödeken gegeben hatte.“

description.en: Hong or jiang (Chinese: 虹; pinyin: hóng or jiàng; Wade–Giles: hung or chiang; lit. 'rainbow') is a Chinese dragon with two heads on each end in Chinese mythology, comparable with Rainbow Serpent legends in various cultures and mythologies.

claims.statement: Hong, or jiang, is a Chinese mythological rainbow dragon with heads at both ends.
claims.statement_id: Hong atau jiang adalah naga pelangi mitologi Tiongkok yang memiliki kepala pada kedua ujung tubuh.
claims.quote: Hong or jiang (Chinese: 虹; pinyin: hóng or jiàng; Wade–Giles: hung or chiang; lit. 'rainbow') is a Chinese dragon with two heads on each end in Chinese mythology, comparable with Rainbow Serpent legends in various cultures and mythologies.

claims.statement: Chinese distinguishes hong, didong, and ni as words related to rainbows.
claims.statement_id: Bahasa Tiongkok membedakan kata hong, didong, dan ni untuk pelangi.
claims.quote: Chinese has three "rainbow" words, regular hóng (虹), literary dìdōng (蝃蝀), and ní (蜺; "secondary rainbow").

claims.statement: Ancient Shang rainbow characters depict an arched two-headed dragon.
claims.statement_id: Aksara pelangi kuno zaman Shang berbentuk naga melengkung berkepala dua.
claims.quote: However, the oldest characters for "rainbow" in Shang dynasty oracle bone script were pictographs of an arched dragon or serpent with open-mouthed heads at both ends.

claims.statement: The Shuowen Jiezi describes the hong character's form as resembling a wug or reptile-like creature.
claims.statement_id: Shuowen Jiezi menggambarkan bentuk aksara hong sebagai mirip makhluk berjenis serangga atau reptil.
claims.quote: The 121 CE Shuowen Jiezi dictionary, the first Chinese character dictionary, described the seal character for hong (虹; 'rainbow') as 狀似蟲; 'shaped like a wug'. Over 18 centuries later, Hopkins described the recently discovered oracle character for 虹.

description.en: The Huay Chivo (Spanish pronunciation: [waj ˈtʃiβo]) is a legendary Maya beast. It is a half-man, half-beast creature, with burning red eyes, and is specific to the Yucatán Peninsula. It is reputed to be an evil sorcerer who can transform himself into a supernatural animal, usually a goat, dog or deer, in order to prey upon livestock. In recent times, it has become associated with the chupacabras. The Huay Chivo is specific to Guatemala, the southeastern Mexican states of Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo. Alleged Huay Chivo activity is sporadically reported in the regional press. Local Maya near the town of Valladolid, in Yucatán, believe the Huay Chivo is an evil sorcerer that is capable of transforming into a goat to do mischief and eat livestock. The Huay Chivo is a local variation of the Mesoamerican Nahual.

description.en: The Huma (Persian: هما, Homâ, Avestan: Homāio), also Homāy or Humo, is a mythical bird of Iranian legends and fables, and continuing as a common motif in Sufi and Diwan poetry. Although there are many legends of the creature, common to all is that the bird is said never to alight on the ground, and instead to live its entire life flying invisibly high above the earth.

description.id: Ibaraki-doji (bahasa Jepang): 茨木童子 atau 茨城童子; arti: anak Ibaraki) adalah salah satu setan berjenis oni, dan dia adalah pemberontak yang terkenal paling ditakuti di Jepang. Dia mengetuai sejumlah daerah milik Shuten-doji sang raja iblis terbesar. Tidak banyak yang diketahui mengenai Ibaraki-doji; bahkan tidak diketahui apakah dia itu pria atau wanita. Pendapat lain mengatakan Ibaraki-doji berjenis kelamin wanita; tetapi, pendapat lainnya mengatakan bahwa wakil penjaga wilayah Shuten-doji adalah pria.
description.en: Ibaraki-dōji (茨木童子 or 茨城童子 "Ibaraki child") is an oni (demon or ogre) featured in tales of the Heian period. In the tales, Ibaraki-dōji is based on Mount Ōe, and once went on a rampage in Kyoto. The "Ibaraki" in his name may refer to Ibaraki, Osaka; "dōji" means "child", but in this context is a demon offspring. Ibaraki-dōji was the most important servant of Shuten-dōji. As for the birthplace, there are theories that it may be Settsu Province (Mio, Ibaraki, Osaka, and Tomatsu, Amagasaki, Hyōgo) or Echigo Province (Niigata, formerly Tochio, now a settlement in Karuizawa, Nagano). Ibaraki-dōji had teeth since birth, and was feared for being a giant. After they became an oni, they met Shuten-dōji and became his subordinate, and together they aimed for the capital. Their gender is ambiguous, in some stories Ibaraki is a kijo (female oni), and in others a male. The female version is theorized to be Shuten-dōji’s lover, son, or his son's lover. The Shuten-dōji gang was based on Mt. Ōe (said to be in Tanba Province, but there are also theories that it may have been at Mt. Ōe, at the boundary between Kyoto and Kameoka). The gang ran amok in the capital, kidnapping families’ girls among other things, but they were destroyed by Minamoto no Yorimitsu and his four vassals, the Four Guardian Kings. However, Ibaraki-dōji was able to escape. According to the legend, Watanabe no Tsuna cut Ibaraki Doji's arm with a tachi named 'Higekiri'. At present, Kitano Tenmangū Shrine owns a tachi 'Onikirimaru' (鬼切丸) handed down as 'Higekiri', which is also called 'Onikiri', 'Onimaru', 'Shishinoko' or 'Tomokiri' based on various legends.

description.en: Iku-Turso (Finnish pronunciation: [ˈikuˌturso], "the eternal giant"; also known as Iku-Tursas, Iki-Tursas, Meritursas, Tursas, Turisas among others) refers to one or multiple giants in Finnish mythology. In the Kalevala, Iku-Turso is a malevolent sea monster. The name Turisas is probably an early loanword from the Proto-Germanic *þurisaz 'giant'. In 1551, Mikael Agricola mentioned Turisas as the god of war: Turisas voiton antoi sodast 'Turisas brought victory in war'. There is no consensus among scholars if the multiple Tursas mentions in runic songs refer to one being or multiple different ones.

description.en: Ilomba is a sea snake with destructive powers in the mythology of the Lozi people of Zambia. It is created by a witch doctor. It is made with their finger nails and blood from their forehead, back, and chest. They mix it in a pan with herbs that were considered to have a magical force. It is usually fed with eggs and porridge when it is young because its fangs are not fully developed. It takes on the identity of the person that owns it. The owner will command it to kill a person. The victim will see the witch doctor's face in place of the Ilomba's, but the other people will view it as a normal snake. It bites into its prey then consumes its soul. If it is killed, the owner feels the pain, and then dies. If the owner dies, it dies. If the witch doctor stops supplying food to it, it will turn on its master and consume them. The only way it can be destroyed is through the witch doctor. When the witch doctor does kill it, they will be constantly haunted by the souls that the Ilomba consumed.

description.en: In the Dove Book and Russian folklore, Indrik or the Indrik-Beast (Russian: Индрик-зверь, romanized: Indrik-zver') is a fabulous beast, the king of all animals, who lives on a mountain known as "The Holy Mountain" where no other foot may tread. When it stirs, the Earth trembles. The word "Indrik" is a distorted version of the Russian word for unicorn (Russian: Единорог, romanized: jedinorog). It is described as a gigantic bull with legs of a deer, the head of a horse and an enormous horn in its snout, making it vaguely similar to a rhinoceros. The Russian folkloric creature gives its name to a synonym of Paraceratherium, Indricotherium, the biggest land mammal ever to live.

description.en: The ipilja-ipilja, or ipilya, is a giant gecko in the mythology of the Anindilyakwa people of Australia. He is considered to be the creator of rain and thunder. The ipilja-ipilja lives with his family, all giant geckos, in the Numarika swamp at the mouth of the Angoroko River of Groote Eylandt. The swamp is considered sacred, and it is believed that anyone who drinks water from the swamp will die. Because of this, the ipilja-ipilja is greatly feared. The wife of the ipilja-ipilja is called the guruina, and together they have a single child. The geckos are all "highly colored," with the ipilja-ipilja being about a hundred feet long and adorned with long hair and whiskers. At the beginning of the monsoon season, the ipilja-ipilja eats the grasses on the edge of the swamp and drinks a large quantity of the swamp water. He then spews the mixture into the sky. The water turns into clouds, and the grass binds the clouds together. The ipilja-ipilja, pleased with his efforts, lets out a roar that becomes thunder. Thus, thunderstorms are created. After the monsoon season, the ipilja-ipilja retires into the swamp. There, except to punishing intruders in his swamp, the ipilja-ipilja rests until the arrival of the next monsoon season. Similar stories can be found on Melville Island and Bathurst Island, where colorful lizards known as the maratji are said to guard their waterholes. Whenever they are being intruded upon, the annoyed maratji will cause floods and thunderstorms. The stories of the ipilja-ipilja and maratji are similar with that of the Rainbow Serpent, a deity popular on the Australian mainland but are not found on Groote Eylandt or Melville Island. It is thought that the myth of the ipilja-ipilja serves as a local replacement for the Rainbow Serpent. Guernea ipilya, an amphipod discovered in the Great Barrier Reef, is named after the ipilja-ipilja.

description.en: Jarita (Sanskrit: जरित, IAST Jaritā) was a certain female bird of the species called Sarngika, whose story is told in the Mahabharata. The saint Mandapala, who returned from the shades because he had no son, assumed the form of a male bird, and by her had four sons. He then abandoned her. In the conflagration of the Khandava Forest she showed great devotion to the protection of her children, and they were eventually saved through the influence of Mandapala over the god of fire. Their names were Jaritari, Sarisrikta, Stambamitra, and Drona. They were "interpreters of the Vedas;" and there are hymns of the Rigveda bearing the names of the second and the third.

description.en: The jentil (or jentilak with the Basque plural), are a race of giants in Basque mythology. This word meaning gentile, from Latin gentilis, was used to refer to pre-Christian civilizations and in particular to the builders of megalithic monuments, to which the other Basque mythical legend the Mairuak are involved too. The jentil were believed to have lived alongside the Basque people. They were hairy and so tall that they could walk in the sea and throw rocks from one mountain to another. This stone throwing has led to several tales and explanations for ancient stone buildings and large isolated rocks. Even the Basque ball game, pilota, is ascribed to these stone-throwers. The tradition lives on in the Basque power games of stone lifting and throwing. Some attributed to the jentil the defeat of Roland in the Battle of Roncevaux, where the Basques defeated the Frankish army by throwing rocks on them. The giants were believed to have created the Neolithic monuments, such as dolmens, found around the Basque Country. They also were said to have invented metallurgy and the saw and first grew wheat, teaching humans to farm. However, they were unwilling to move to the valleys from the mountains, with a certain unwillingness to progress. They disappeared into the earth under a dolmen in the Arratzaren valley in Navarra when a portentous luminous cloud – perhaps a star – appeared, said to have heralded the birth of Christ (Kixmi) and the end of the jentil age. Other stories say jentil threw themselves from a mountain. Only Olentzero remained, a giant who appears at Christmas and is reproduced as straw dolls. There are many structures and places around the Basque Country with jentil in their name, generally referring to pagan or ancient places, supposedly built by the jentil. Dolmens are jentilarri or jentiletxe, harrespil are jentilbaratz, caves can be jentilzulo or jentilkoba.

description.id: Jorogumo (bahasa Jepang Kanji: 絡新婦, Hiragana: じょろうぐも) adalah makhluk sejenis yokai dalam cerita rakyat Jepang yang menyerupai laba-laba. Cerita yokai ini sudah ada sejak Zaman Edo dan dikatakan ia dapat mengubah bentuknya menjadi wanita cantik. Menurut legenda, Jorogumo memiliki ukuran tubuh yang besar dengan punggung panjang dan ramping, bagian ujung belakangnya runcing, memiliki tungkai hitam panjang serta benang lengket berwarna kuning. Nama jorogumo ditemukan pada beberapa tulisan dari Zaman Edo seperti Taihei-Hyakumonogatari (太平百物語) dan Tonoigusa (宿直草).
description.en: Jorōgumo (Japanese: 絡新婦 (kanji), じょろうぐも (hiragana)) is a type of yōkai, a creature of Japanese folklore. It can shapeshift into a beautiful woman, so the kanji that represent its actual meaning are 女郎蜘蛛 (lit. 'woman-spider'); the kanji which are used to write it instead, 絡新婦 (lit. 'entangling newlywed woman') have a jukujikun pronunciation that is related to the meaning, but not the sound of the word. In Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, it is depicted as a spider woman manipulating small fire-breathing spiders. Jorōgumo can also refer to some species of spiders, such as the Nephila and Argiope spiders. Japanese-speaking entomologists use the katakana form of jorōgumo (ジョロウグモ) to refer exclusively to the spider species Trichonephila clavata, and this has been adopted into English as "Joro spider".

description.en: Kalaviṅka (Sanskrit: कलविंक kalaviṅka; Pali: karavika; Chinese: 迦陵頻伽; pinyin: Jiālíngpínqié; Japanese: 迦陵頻伽, romanized: Karyōbinga, Korean: 가릉빈가; Vietnamese: Ca Lăng Tần Già; Burmese: ကရဝိက် karawik; Thai: การเวก; Khmer: ករវិក karavik; Malay: karawek) is a fantastical immortal creature in Buddhism, with a human head and a bird's torso, with long flowing tail. The kalaviṅka is said to dwell in the Western pure land and is reputed to preach the Dharma with its fine voice. It is said to sing while still unhatched within its eggshell. Its voice is a descriptor of the Buddha's voice. In the Japanese text, it goes by various titles such as myōonchō (妙音鳥, "exquisite sounding bird"), kōonchō (好音鳥, "goodly sounding bird") among others. Edward H. Schafer notes that in East Asian religious art the Kalaviṅka is often confused with the Kinnara, which is also a half-human half-bird hybrid mythical creature, but that the two are actually distinct and unrelated.

description.id: Kamadenu (Dewanagari: कामधेनु; ,IAST: Kāmadhenu,; [kaːmɐˈdʱeːnʊ]), juga dikenal dengan nama Surabi (Dewanagari: सुरभी; ,IAST: Surabhī, सुरभी), adalah nama dewi sapi dalam agama Hindu yang diyakini sebagai ibu bagi semua sapi. Ia adalah sapi ajaib yang mampu memenuhi apa pun yang diinginkan oleh pemeliharanya, dan sering kali dikisahkan sebagai ibu bagi sapi-sapi lainnya. Dalam ikonografi, ia biasanya dilambangkan sebagai sapi putih dengan kepala dan payudara wanita, bersayap burung, dan berekor merak, atau digambarkan sebagai sapi putih dengan berbagai dewa-dewi terkandung dalam tubuhnya. Kamadenu tidak dipuja secara khusus sebagai seorang dewi. Namun, ia dihormati dengan cara menghormati sapi-sapi sebagaimana yang dilakukan oleh umat Hindu, sebab diyakini bahwa ia merupakan lambang kesuburan dan kemakmuran. Dalam pustaka Hindu terdapat kisah yang berbeda-beda tentang kemunculan Kamadenu. Beberapa kitab mencatat bahwa ia tercipta dari pengadukan lautan susu. Pustaka yang lain menyebutkan bahwa ia merupakan salah satu putri Daksa, dan menjadi istri Resi Kasyapa. Bahkan dalam kitab yang lain menyebutkan bahwa ia merupakan sapi milik Jamadagni atau Wasista, dan raja-raja yang mencoba untuk merebutnya dari sang resi akan menghadapi konsekuensi yang berat. Kamadenu memiliki peran penting dalam menyediakan susu dan hasil olahan susu untuk digunakan dalam upacara yang dilaksanakan pemiliknya; ia juga mampu menciptakan laskar hebat untuk melindungi pemeliharanya. Selain tinggal di asrama resi, ia juga dikisahkan tinggal di Goloka (dunia para sapi), dan Patala, alam bawah tanah.
description.en: Kamadhenu (Sanskrit: कामधेनु, [kaːmɐˈdʱeːnʊ], Kāmadhenu), also known as Surabhi (सुरभि, Surabhi or सुरभी, Surabhī), is a divine bovine-goddess described in Hinduism as the mother of all cows. She is a miraculous cow of plenty who provides her owner whatever they desire and is often portrayed as the mother of other cattle. In iconography, she is generally depicted as a white cow with a female head and breasts, the wings of a bird, and the tail of a peafowl or as a white cow containing various deities within her body. Kamadhenu is not worshipped independently as a goddess. Rather, she is honored by the Hindu veneration of cows, who are regarded as her earthly embodiments. Hindu scriptures provide diverse accounts of the birth of Kamadhenu. While some narrate that she emerged from the churning of the cosmic ocean, others describe her as the daughter of the creator god Daksha, and as the wife of the sage Kashyapa. Still other scriptures narrate that Kamadhenu was in the possession of either Jamadagni or Vashista (both ancient sages), and that kings who tried to steal her from the sage ultimately faced dire consequences for their actions. Kamadhenu plays the important role of providing milk and milk products to be used in her sage-master's oblations; she is also capable of producing fierce warriors to protect him. In addition to dwelling in the sage's hermitage, she is also described as dwelling in Goloka—the realm of the cows—and Pātāla, the netherworld.

description.en: In Meitei mythology and Sanamahism, the indigenous religion of Manipur, Kanglā shā (Meitei: ꯀꯡꯂꯥ ꯁꯥ, lit. 'beast of the Kangla') is a sacred guardian beast with a lion's body and a two-horned dragon's head. It is a royal symbol of the Meitei royalties (Ningthouja dynasty). The most remarkable statues dedicated to "Kangla Sa" stand inside the Kangla. In Meitei traditional race competitions, winners of the race are declared only after symbolically touching the statue of the dragon "Kangla Sha".

claims.statement_id: Makhluk itu merupakan lambang kerajaan Meitei.
claims.quote: It is a royal symbol of the Meitei royalties (Ningthouja dynasty).

claims.statement: Traditional race winners are declared after symbolically touching its statue.
claims.statement_id: Pemenang perlombaan tradisional ditentukan setelah menyentuh patungnya secara simbolis.
claims.quote: In Meitei traditional race competitions, winners of the race are declared only after symbolically touching the statue of the dragon "Kangla Sha".

claims.statement: Raja Nara Singh reconstructs two Kangla Sha statues in 1844.
claims.statement_id: Raja Nara Singh membangun kembali dua patung Kangla Sha pada 1844.
claims.quote: During the months of June and July in the year 1844, Meitei king Raja Nara Singh (Meitei: ꯅꯤꯡꯊꯧ ꯅꯔꯁꯤꯡꯍ) reconstructed the two statues of the Kangla Sha dragons once again.

claims.statement: British troops destroy the two statues with artillery fire on 20 July 1891.
claims.statement_id: Pasukan Inggris menghancurkan dua patung itu dengan tembakan artileri pada 20 Juli 1891.
claims.quote: During the British conquest of the Anglo Manipur War of 1891, the British forces led by Captain Allen demolished the two statues of the Kangla Sha dragons by blasting them by artillery fire into pieces on 20 July 1891.

description.en: A kapre is a mythical creature with a human-like appearance that is often described as a tree giant, being a tall, dark-coloured, hairy, and muscular creature. In Philippine folklore, kapres are giants that often dwell atop fruitless tree branches and smoke large cigars, behaving mischievously but benignly around nearby travelers.

claims.statement: The kapre is a humanlike mythical creature described as a tall, dark, hairy, muscular tree giant; in Philippine folklore kapres dwell atop fruitless tree branches, smoke large cigars and are mischievous but benign toward travellers.
claims.statement_id: Kapre adalah makhluk mitos mirip manusia yang digambarkan sebagai raksasa pohon yang tinggi, gelap, berbulu, dan berotot; dalam cerita rakyat Filipina kapre tinggal di dahan pohon tak berbuah, mengisap cerutu besar, dan usil tetapi tidak jahat terhadap pejalan.
claims.quote: A kapre is a mythical creature with a human-like appearance that is often described as a tree giant, being a tall, dark-coloured, hairy, and muscular creature. In Philippine folklore, kapres are giants that often dwell atop fruitless tree branches and smoke large cigars, behaving mischievously but benignly around nearby travelers.

claims.statement: Kapre comes from Arabic kafir (Spanish cafre), 'non-believer', brought to the Philippines by the Spanish; a synonym is agtà; modern kapre portrayals evolved from racially prejudiced depictions of Negrito tribes by Christianized lowlanders in the Spanish period.
claims.statement_id: Istilah kapre berasal dari bahasa Arab kafir (Spanyol cafre), 'orang tak beriman', dibawa ke Filipina oleh orang Spanyol; sinonim kapre adalah agtà; penggambaran kapre modern berkembang dari penggambaran berprasangka rasial terhadap suku Negrito oleh kelompok dataran rendah yang dikristenkan pada masa Spanyol.
claims.quote: The term kapre comes from the Arabic kafir (Spanish cafre), meaning a non-believer in Arabic (usually referring to atheists/idolists). The term was later brought to the Philippines by the Spanish

claims.statement: Kapres are believed nocturnal and omnivorous, not necessarily evil, but vengeful if their tree is cut down; a kapre attracted to a woman may follow her throughout life.
claims.statement_id: Kapre dipercaya aktif malam hari dan omnivora, tidak selalu jahat, tetapi dapat menjadi pendendam bila pohon tempat tinggalnya ditebang; kapre yang tertarik pada perempuan dapat terus mengikutinya seumur hidup.
claims.quote: Kapres are believed to be nocturnal and omnivorous. They are not necessarily considered to be evil. However, they may turn vengeful when the tree that they are inhabiting is cut down.

claims.statement: Kapres, also called agtà, play pranks, making travellers lose their way in mountains or woods, and can confuse people even in familiar surroundings.
claims.statement_id: Kapre, juga disebut agtà, suka mempermainkan orang, membuat pejalan tersesat di gunung atau hutan, dan dapat membingungkan orang bahkan di lingkungan yang sudah dikenalnya.
claims.quote: Kapres, also called agtà, are said to play pranks on people, frequently making travelers become disoriented and lose their way in the mountains or in the woods. They are also believed to possess the ability to confuse people, even when they are in their own familiar surroundings.

claims.statement: According to Jordan Clark, the name's leading etymology begins with Arabic kāfir, a religious term for an unbeliever, adopted by Portuguese and Spanish as cafre.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Jordan Clark, asal kata kapre bermula dari kata Arab kāfir, istilah keagamaan untuk orang tak beriman, yang diadopsi bahasa Portugis dan Spanyol sebagai cafre.
claims.quote: The leading etymological path begins with Arabic kāfir, a religious term for an unbeliever or one who rejects faith. Portuguese and Spanish adopted related forms such as cafre.

claims.statement: Jordan Clark stresses that living Indigenous peoples must not be confused with folklore beings just because colonial accounts used the same name.
claims.statement_id: Jordan Clark menekankan bahwa masyarakat adat yang masih hidup tidak boleh disamakan dengan makhluk folklor hanya karena catatan kolonial memakai nama yang sama.
claims.quote: At the same time, living Indigenous peoples must not be confused with beings in folklore simply because a colonial or lowland account used the same name. The history of a label is not a definition of a people.

claims.statement: The record shows a colonial human label in 19th-century dictionaries, a clearly folkloric kapre in 1906, and traits of regional beings like the pugot being compared or transferred soon after.
claims.statement_id: Catatan yang ada menunjukkan label manusia masa kolonial dalam kamus abad kesembilan belas, kapre yang jelas bersifat folklor pada 1906, dan bukti bahwa ciri makhluk daerah seperti pugot kemudian dibandingkan atau dialihkan kepadanya.
claims.quote: it shows a colonial human label in nineteenth-century dictionaries, a clearly folkloric Kapre in 1906, and evidence that traits associated with regional beings such as the Pugot were being compared or transferred soon afterward.

claims.statement: Signs of a kapre include rustling branches without strong wind, loud laughter from an unseen being, heavy smoke from a treetop and big red glaring eyes in a tree at night.
claims.statement_id: Tanda kehadiran kapre antara lain dahan bergoyang meski angin tidak kencang, tawa keras dari sosok tak terlihat, asap tebal dari puncak pohon, dan mata merah besar menyala di pohon pada malam hari.
claims.quote: Some more examples would be hearing loud laughter coming from an unseen being, witnessing much smoke from the top of a tree, seeing big red glaring eyes during night time from a tree

description.id: Kasha (かしゃ) adalah sejenis bake-neko atau kucing monster dengan tubuh bipedal seukuran di atas tinggi rata-rata manusia. Kasha merupakan salah satu yokai yang banyak digambarkan dalam cerita rakyat Jepang. Beberapa diantaranya ia muncul dalam karya periode Edo Boso Monroku (The Musings of Boso) tahun 1833, Shin Otogi Boko tahun 1683, Shokoku Hyaku Monogatari (One Hundred Stories from Various Countries) tahun 1677, dan karya pada periode Heian Konjaku Monogatarishu (Anthology of Tales from the Past). Dalam budaya populer ia muncul sebagai monster dalam film animasi tahun 1970 berjudul Kasha.
description.en: The kasha (obsolete: kwasha; Japanese: 火車, lit. 'fire cart', "burning chariot" or 化車, 'changed wheel') in Japanese folklore is a yōkai said to steal corpses. It is now generally regarded to be a monster in cat-form, though earlier archetypes made them demon-like.

claims.statement: Kasha is a Japanese yōkai said to steal corpses.
claims.statement_id: Kasha adalah yōkai Jepang yang dikisahkan mencuri jenazah.
claims.quote: in Japanese folklore is a yōkai said to steal corpses. It is now generally regarded to be a monster in cat-form

claims.statement: Modern depictions are often cat-like while earlier forms were demon-like.
claims.statement_id: Penggambaran sekarang kerap menyerupai kucing, sedangkan bentuk awal lebih mirip iblis.
claims.quote: It is now generally regarded to be a monster in cat-form, though earlier archetypes made them demon-like.

claims.statement: The earlier kasha was a fiery vehicle carrying sinners to Buddhist hell.
claims.statement_id: Makna awal kasha ialah kendaraan api yang membawa pendosa ke neraka Buddhis.
claims.quote: The kasha was originally neither an animal- nor man-like monster, but a fire vehicle (cf. hi no kuruma) assigned the mission of conveying the sinful to Buddhist hell.

claims.statement: Early modern depictions also associated it with hell wardens or the thunder god.
claims.statement_id: Pada masa awal modern, kasha juga dipahami sebagai penjaga neraka atau dewa petir.
claims.quote: The kasha as yōkai in the early modern period (16th century) was originally conceived of as the demon-like beings

claims.statement: Conflation with corpse-stealing nekomata tales helped produce its cat form.
claims.statement_id: Perpaduan dengan kisah nekomata yang mencuri mayat mendorong wujud kucingnya.
claims.quote: But due to conflation with the legends of the devil-cat (nekomata) stealing cadavers, the kasha came to be seen as a cat-like yōkai in the late 17th century.

claims.statement: Kasha is often associated with dark clouds and thunder.
claims.statement_id: Kemunculan kasha kerap dikaitkan dengan awan gelap dan guntur.
claims.quote: The kasha is often said to appear with dark clouds, thunderclaps, or thunderstorms.

description.en: The Kayeri is a giant, plant-like humanoid cryptid from the folklore of the Cuiba people of Colombia and Venezuela. Visual descriptors for the beings are varied, ranging from appearing like a giant with a large, mushroom-like hat to appearing like a ficus, making the physiology of the being primarily cryptobotanic in nature. It is said all the mushrooms of the forest are aspects of the creature, and not unlike mushrooms, Kayeri are said to appear after significant rain and at the base of trees, often dormant after significant sunshine. The Kayeri diet consists solely of cows, and the Cuiban people often attribute the disappearance or deaths of their cattle to the Kayeri who are strong enough to carry bovine away. It is said that the most effective way to kill them is to shoot them in the kidney with a bone-tipped arrow.

claims.statement: The Kayeri is a giant plant-like humanoid cryptid from folklore of the Cuiba people in Colombia and Venezuela.
claims.statement_id: Kayeri adalah kriptid humanoid raksasa mirip tanaman dari cerita rakyat suku Cuiba di Colombia dan Venezuela.
claims.quote: The Kayeri is a giant, plant-like humanoid cryptid from the folklore of the Cuiba people of Colombia and Venezuela.

claims.statement: Descriptions range from a giant with a mushroom hat to resembling a ficus, exhibiting cryptobotanic physiology.
claims.statement_id: Penggambaran fisik Kayeri bervariasi dari raksasa bertopi jamur besar hingga menyerupai pohon ficus.
claims.quote: Visual descriptors for the beings are varied, ranging from appearing like a giant with a large, mushroom-like hat to appearing like a ficus, making the physiology of the being primarily cryptobotanic in nature.

claims.statement: All forest mushrooms are aspects of the creature, appearing after heavy rain at tree bases and going dormant in sunshine.
claims.statement_id: Semua jamur hutan dipandang sebagai bagian dari makhluk ini yang muncul setelah hujan lebat di pangkal pohon.
claims.quote: It is said all the mushrooms of the forest are aspects of the creature, and not unlike mushrooms, Kayeri are said to appear after significant rain and at the base of trees, often dormant after significant sunshine.

claims.statement: The Kayeri feeds on cows, and cattle disappearances are blamed on its ability to carry bovine away.
claims.statement_id: Makanan Kayeri adalah sapi, dan hilangnya ternak sering dikaitkan dengan kekuatannya mengangkat ternak.
claims.quote: The Kayeri diet consists solely of cows, and the Cuiban people often attribute the disappearance or deaths of their cattle to the Kayeri who are strong enough to carry bovine away.

description.en: Khamot (Thai: โขมด, pronounced [kʰà.mòːt]) is a type of ghost in Thai folklore. The term is borrowed from the Khmer word khmaoch (ខ្មោច, pronounced [khmōch], lit. 'ghost in general'). It is considered a spirit related to Krasue and Phong ghosts.

claims.statement: Khamot (โขมด) is a ghost of Thai folklore; its name is borrowed from Khmer khmaoch, 'ghost in general', and it is considered related to the krasue and phong ghosts.
claims.statement_id: Khamot (โขมด) adalah hantu dalam cerita rakyat Thailand; namanya dipinjam dari kata Khmer khmaoch, 'hantu secara umum', dan ia dianggap berkerabat dengan krasue dan hantu phong.
claims.quote: is a type of ghost in Thai folklore. The term is borrowed from the Khmer word khmaoch

claims.statement: In some accounts khamot appears as a floating, flickering light at night, especially in damp or marshy areas, misleading forest travellers into thinking someone ahead carries a torch or there is a fire; approached, it vanishes and reappears all around.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebagian kisah khamot tampak sebagai bola cahaya melayang yang berkedip di malam hari, terutama di daerah lembap atau berawa, dan menyesatkan pengembara di hutan seolah ada orang membawa obor atau api di depan; saat didekati cahaya itu lenyap lalu muncul mengelilingi.
claims.quote: In some accounts, it appears as a floating ball of light, a large flickering glow seen at night, especially in damp or marshy areas. It is said to lure travelers in the forest into losing their way, making them believe that someone ahead is carrying a torch or that there is a fire.

claims.statement: Per the Royal Institute Dictionary, the phenomenon is scientifically explained as methane from decaying organic matter igniting in the air; it also groups khamot with the krasue and phong ghosts.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kamus Royal Institute, secara ilmiah gejala ini dijelaskan sebagai gas metana dari pembusukan bahan organik yang dapat menyala di udara; kamus itu juga menggolongkan khamot bersama krasue dan hantu phong.
claims.quote: Scientifically, this phenomenon is explained as methane gas produced by the decomposition of organic matter, which can ignite in the air and appear as flickering lights in the dark.

claims.statement: In some regions khamot is a forest spirit seen as floating light; in others a malevolent ghost deceiving travellers by shapeshifting.
claims.statement_id: Di beberapa daerah khamot dianggap roh hutan berupa cahaya melayang, di daerah lain hantu jahat yang menipu pengembara dengan berganti wujud.
claims.quote: In others, it is considered a malevolent ghost that deceives and haunts travelers by shapeshifting into various forms.

claims.statement: In Lamphun, northern Thailand, the Loy Khamot tradition is held at the twelfth lunar month's full moon, coinciding with Loy Krathong, with floating lanterns sparkling like khamot's lights.
claims.statement_id: Di Provinsi Lamphun, Thailand utara, ada tradisi Loy Khamot pada purnama bulan kedua belas, bertepatan dengan Loy Krathong, dengan lentera terapung yang berkilau seperti cahaya khamot.
claims.quote: In Lamphun province, northern Thailand, there is a local tradition called Loy Khamot (ลอยโขมด), held during the full moon of the twelfth lunar month, which coincides with the Loy Krathong festival

description.en: In Nepalese folklore or mythology, kichkanya (Nepali: किच्कन्या) also referred to as Kichkandi (Nepali: किच्कन्डी) is a spirit of a woman that is latched to an uncremated part of her dead body, usually a bone. They are generally known to be solitary spirits that haunt a particular location. Children often grow up hearing the stories of such tortured souls of women who wander the site of their untimely death. These women while alive were treated unfairly in some manner or died during childbirth or pregnancy. According to sightings, they are supposed to have unusually long black hair, pale and bony complexion and dressed up in a red bridal dress. It is said that they can be identified by looking at their feet, which face backward. People usually describe them as alluring and young female, who lures a lonely male traveler and saps their life force. The victims are said to turn out drained of their life and skinny. According to other tales told by locals and cab drivers, these spirits are also known to hitchhike late at night. When the drivers of the vehicle or motorbike follow her directions, they end up in cremation grounds in a temple or a cemetery.

claims.statement: Kichkandi is a woman's spirit in Nepalese folklore attached to an uncremated part of her body.
claims.statement_id: Kichkandi adalah roh perempuan dalam cerita rakyat Nepal yang melekat pada bagian tubuhnya yang belum dikremasi.
claims.quote: In Nepalese folklore or mythology, kichkanya (Nepali: किच्कन्या) also referred to as Kichkandi (Nepali: किच्कन्डी) is a spirit of a woman that is latched to an uncremated part of her dead body, usually a bone.

claims.statement: Tales place her at the site of an untimely death.
claims.statement_id: Cerita menempatkannya di lokasi kematian yang tidak wajar.
claims.quote: Children often grow up hearing the stories of such tortured souls of women who wander the site of their untimely death.

claims.statement: She is said to have long black hair, a pale complexion and red bridal clothing.
claims.statement_id: Ia dikatakan berambut panjang hitam, berkulit pucat, dan memakai pakaian pengantin merah.
claims.quote: they are supposed to have unusually long black hair, pale and bony complexion and dressed up in a red bridal dress.

claims.statement: Her feet are said to face backward.
claims.statement_id: Kakinya dikatakan menghadap ke belakang.
claims.quote: It is said that they can be identified by looking at their feet, which face backward.

claims.statement: She lures a solitary male traveller and drains his life force.
claims.statement_id: Ia memikat pelancong laki-laki sendirian dan menyerap daya hidupnya.
claims.quote: People usually describe them as alluring and young female, who lures a lonely male traveler and saps their life force. The victims are said to turn out drained of their life and skinny. According to other tales told by locals and cab drivers, these spirits are also known to hitchhike late at night.

claims.statement: The film Bhoot Police portrays Maya's tea estate as haunted by a kichkandi.
claims.statement_id: Film Bhoot Police menggambarkan perkebunan teh Maya dihantui kichkandi.
claims.quote: In Bhoot Police, a 2021 Bollywood film, the tea estate of the character Maya(played by Yami Gautam) is haunted by a kichkandi.

description.en: The kimpurushas (Sanskrit: किंपुरुष, romanized: Kimpuruṣa) are a race of beings featured in Hindu literature, described as possessing the bodies of human beings and lion heads. They are associated with, and sometimes considered the same as the kinnaras, though some Puranas distinguish between them. They are attendants of the god of wealth, Kubera.

claims.statement: Kimpurushas are beings in Hindu literature described as human-bodied with lion heads.
claims.statement_id: Kimpurusha adalah kelompok makhluk dalam sastra Hindu yang memiliki tubuh manusia dan kepala singa.
claims.quote: The kimpurushas (Sanskrit: किंपुरुष, romanized: Kimpuruṣa) are a race of beings featured in Hindu literature, described as possessing the bodies of human beings and lion heads. They are associated with, and sometimes considered the same as the kinnaras, though some Puranas distinguish between them. They are attendants of the god of wealth, Kubera.

claims.statement: They are associated with kinnaras, but some Puranas distinguish the two.
claims.statement_id: Mereka dikaitkan dengan kinnara, tetapi beberapa Purana membedakan keduanya.
claims.quote: They are associated with, and sometimes considered the same as the kinnaras, though some Puranas distinguish between them.

claims.statement: They serve Kubera, the wealth god.
claims.statement_id: Mereka merupakan pelayan Kubera, dewa kekayaan.
claims.quote: They are attendants of the god of wealth, Kubera.

claims.statement: Brahma is said to create kimpurushas and kinnaras from his reflected image.
claims.statement_id: Brahma dikatakan menciptakan kimpurusha dan kinnara dari pantulan dirinya.
claims.quote: Brahma is described to have created the kimpurushas and the kinnaras from his own reflected image.

claims.statement: They praise Narasimha after he kills Hiranyakashipu.
claims.statement_id: Mereka memuji Narasimha setelah ia membunuh Hiranyakashipu.
claims.quote: The kimpurushas, along with a number of other beings, praise the glory of the Narasimha avatar of Vishnu after he slays Hiranyakashipu.

claims.statement: Budha changes women into kimpurushis and instructs them to dwell on a mountain.
claims.statement_id: Budha mengubah sejumlah perempuan menjadi kimpurushi dan menyuruh mereka tinggal di gunung.
claims.quote: Budha transforms a number of women into kimpurushis (female kimpurushas) and instructs them to make a mountain their abode and take kimpurushas for their consorts.

description.id: Kirtimuka (Dewanagari: कीर्तिमुख; ,IAST: kīrtimukha,; arti: "muka yang megah") adalah nama makhluk mitologis berwajah monster, dengan taring panjang, mulut menganga, dan lazim ditampilkan sebagai ukiran dalam arsitektur kuil Hindu di Nepal, India, dan Asia Tenggara, dan juga di sejumlah arsitektur Buddhis. Tidak seperti makhluk mitologi Hindu lainnya, seperti monster laut Makara, kirtimuka memang tercipta sebagai ragam hias pada bangunan, yang memiliki mitos asal mula di kitab Skandapurana dan Siwapurana.
description.en: Kirtimukha (Sanskrit: कीर्तिमुख ,kīrtimukha, also kīrttimukha, a bahuvrihi compound translating to "glorious face") is the name of a swallowing fierce face with huge fangs, and gaping mouth, very common in the iconography of Hindu temple architecture in South Asia and Southeast Asia, and often also found in Buddhist architecture. Unlike other Hindu legendary creatures, for example the sea-dwelling makara, the kirtimukha is essentially an ornamental motif in art, which has its origin in a legend from the Skanda Purana and the Shiva Purana.

claims.statement: Kirtimukha is a fierce face with large fangs and a gaping mouth in Hindu and Buddhist architecture.
claims.statement_id: Kirtimukha adalah wajah ganas bertaring besar dan bermulut menganga dalam arsitektur Hindu dan Buddha.
claims.quote: is the name of a swallowing fierce face with huge fangs, and gaping mouth, very common in the iconography of Hindu temple architecture in South Asia and Southeast Asia, and often also found in Buddhist architecture.

claims.statement: This ornamental motif has a narrative origin in the Skanda Purana and Shiva Purana.
claims.statement_id: Motif hias ini memiliki asal kisah dalam Skanda Purana dan Shiva Purana.
claims.quote: Unlike other Hindu legendary creatures, for example the sea-dwelling makara, the kirtimukha is essentially an ornamental motif in art, which has its origin in a legend from the Skanda Purana and the Shiva Purana.

claims.statement: Mukha means face and kirti means fame or glory.
claims.statement_id: Mukha berarti wajah dan kirti berarti kemasyhuran atau kemuliaan.
claims.quote: The word mukha in Sanskrit refers to the face while kīrti means "fame, glory".  The story of Kirtimukha begins when the asura king Jalandhara, who "by virtue of extraordinary austerities ... accumulated to himself irresistible powers." In a burst of pride, he sent forth his messenger, the Hindu deity Rahu, whose main task is eclipsing the moon, to challenge Shiva. "The challenge ...

claims.statement: Zimmer interprets it as an apotropaic demon mask and guardian of the threshold.
claims.statement_id: Zimmer menafsirkannya sebagai topeng demon penolak bahaya dan penjaga ambang.
claims.quote: The Kirtimukha is often used as a motif surmounting the pinnacle of a temple or the image of a deity, especially in South Indian architecture. As Zimmer writes, "Kirtimukha serves primarily as an apotropaic demon-mask, a gruesome, awe-inspiring guardian of the threshold."

claims.statement: The motif decorates sanctum doorway lintels, often showing only the upper jaw and upper face.
claims.statement_id: Motif ini menghias lintel pintu ruang suci, sering hanya memperlihatkan rahang atas dan bagian atas wajah.
claims.quote: This fierce face with bulging eyes sits also as an embellishment over the lintel of the gate to the inner sanctum in many Hindu temples ... very often only the upper jaw and top of the face is visible

claims.statement: Singapore's NHB calls kirtimukha an auspicious face of glory in South and Southeast Asian Hindu Buddhist temple architecture.
claims.statement_id: NHB Singapura menyebut kirtimukha sebagai wajah kemuliaan yang mujur dalam arsitektur kuil Hindu-Buddha Asia Selatan dan Tenggara.
claims.quote: The kirtimukha or auspicious face of glory is popular icon in South and Southeast Asian Hindu-Buddhist temple architecture.

description.en: According to Swedish legend, the Knights of Ålleberg are ghosts of twelve knights who died at the Battle of Åsle in a 1389. The legend is an example of the king asleep in mountain motif in folklore.

claims.statement: According to Swedish legend, the Knights of Ålleberg are the ghosts of twelve knights killed at the Battle of Åsle in 1389; the legend exemplifies the king-asleep-in-the-mountain motif.
claims.statement_id: Menurut legenda Swedia (Swedish), Ksatria Ålleberg (Knights of Ålleberg) adalah arwah dua belas ksatria yang gugur dalam Pertempuran Åsle (Battle of Åsle) tahun 1389; legenda ini contoh motif raja yang tidur di dalam gunung.
claims.quote: According to Swedish legend, the Knights of Ålleberg are ghosts of twelve knights who died at the Battle of Åsle in a 1389. The legend is an example of the king asleep in mountain motif in folklore.

claims.statement: The Battle of Åsle, also called the Battle of Falköping, took place in or near Falköping on 24 February (or August) 1389 between the forces of Albert, King of Sweden, and Margaret I of Denmark.
claims.statement_id: Pertempuran Åsle, juga disebut Pertempuran Falköping, terjadi di atau sekitar Falköping pada 24 Februari (atau Agustus) 1389 antara pasukan Albert, Raja Swedia (Sweden), dan Margaret I dari Denmark (Denmark).
claims.quote: The legend concerns knights who died at the Battle of Åsle, sometimes known as the Battle of Falköping, that took place in or around Falköping on 24 February (or August) 1389 between the forces of Albert, King of Sweden and Margaret I of Denmark.

claims.statement: The story has the ghosts trapped in Ålleberg mountain, awaiting a new war to wake them to fight for the country; the mountain is also thought to host trolls.
claims.statement_id: Menurut kisahnya arwah-arwah itu terkurung di dalam gunung Ålleberg, menunggu perang baru membangunkan mereka untuk berjuang menyelamatkan negeri; gunung itu juga dianggap dihuni troll.
claims.quote: The story says that the ghosts are trapped inside the Ålleberg mountain, waiting for a new war to wake them up so they can fight to save the country. The mountain is also thought to play host to trolls.

claims.statement: The commonest legend tells of a farmer taking grain to market in Falköping; a man asked to buy the whole load, and the farmer followed him into a hall in the mountain where the knights slept in full armour.
claims.statement_id: Legenda paling umum menceritakan petani yang membawa muatan gandum ke pasar Falköping; seorang lelaki minta membeli semua muatannya, dan petani itu mengikutinya ke aula di dalam gunung, tempat para ksatria tidur berbaju zirah lengkap.
claims.quote: Den vanligaste av sägnerna om Ållebergs ryttare handlar om en bonde som for med ett lass säd till marknaden i Falköping. description.en: Konaki-jiji (子泣き爺; also romanized konaki-jijii or konakijijii) is a yōkai — a supernatural creature from Japanese folklore — originating in the mountain regions of Tokushima Prefecture on the island of Shikoku. The name is typically translated as "old man crying like a baby" or "baby-crying old man," combining ko naki (子泣き, "child crying") with jijii (爺, "old man"). It is one of the most widely recognized yōkai in Japan, documented in major folklorist compilations, depicted visually for the first time by manga artist Shigeru Mizuki, and featured across decades of Japanese popular culture. The konaki-jiji is notable for its deceptive method of attack: it lures compassionate travelers by mimicking the sound of an infant crying in the wilderness, then, once picked up, becomes supernaturally heavy, crushing its victim to death.

description.en: The Koolakamba or Kooloo-Kamba is a purported hybrid species of chimpanzees and gorillas. This alleged hybrid ape species has been reported in Africa as early as the mid 19th century. No empirical evidence has been found to substantiate the existence of the creature. The Koolakamba was referenced in the mid-19th century in French work by Franquet (1852, as cited by Shea, 1984) and in some descriptive work of Paul Du Chaillu from 1860, 1861, 1867, and 1899, some of which was republished in 1969 (Explorations and Adventures in Equatorial Africa).

description.en: The koromodako (ころもだこ/衣蛸; "clothing octopus") is a yōkai in the Japanese folklore. Although in the guise of a small octopus, it is said to expand and envelop boats and people. The lore is localized in northern Kyoto Prefecture, vaguely described as promontory areas (jutting into Wakasa Bay), though also pinpointed to a village (Sodeshi) at the northern tip of Tango Peninsula.

description.en: Krahang (Thai: กระหัง, pronounced [krā.hǎŋ]; or กระหาง, [krā.hǎːŋ]) is a male spirit of the Thai folklore. It manifests itself as a shirtless man, wearing a traditional loincloth, who flies in the night. Krahang uses two large kradong (กระด้ง), round rice winnowing baskets, to fly in the night in rural areas of Thailand. It also often rides a sak tam khao (สากตำข้าว), the long wooden pestle of a traditional manual rice pounder.

description.en: The Krepel, also known as the Bytom Dragon (Polish: smok bytomski; Silesian: bytōmski smok), is a legendary Polish dragon said to have inhabited the forests near Bytom in Upper Silesia. description.en: Kui (Chinese: 夔; pinyin: kuí; Wade–Giles: k'uei) is a polysemous figure in ancient Chinese mythology. Classic texts use this name for the legendary musician Kui who invented music and dancing; for the one-legged mountain demon or rain-god Kui variously said to resemble a Chinese dragon, a drum, or a monkey with a human face; and for the Kuiniu wild yak or buffalo.

description.en: In Japanese folklore, the Kunekune (くねくね; 'wriggling body') is a fictional being typically described as having a slender, white, paper (or fabric-like) humanoid shape, which is usually said to appear in fields on hot summer days. The story originated on the Internet as a Japanese urban legend, being first mentioned on websites in 2001. Its name, Kunekune, is derived from its alleged behavior of wiggling its limbs. The Kunekune may be explained by people being confused by the appearance of scarecrows or wick drains.

description.en: Kussie (クッシー, Kusshī) is a Japanese lake monster (a cryptid) said to be living in Hokkaidō's Lake Kussharo on the northern island of Hokkaido. The name "Kussie" is ostensibly inspired by "Nessie", the nickname for the Loch Ness Monster in Scotland. Lake Kussharo, where Kussie is said to live, is situated within Akan National Park in eastern Hokkaido. The lake is a caldera lake, meaning it was formed in the crater of a volcano. This lake is notable for its connection to Ainu culture, as its name derives from the Ainu word "Kuccharo", which translates to "The place where a lake becomes a river and the river flows out". A statue of Kussie on the shore of Lake Kussharo signifies the figure's prominence in local culture. Similar to other lake monster tales around the world, stories about Kussie contribute to local folklore and attract curiosity and tourism to the area.

description.en: La Guita Xica (Catalan pronunciation: [lə ˈɣitə ˈʃikə]) is a dragon that appears amongst the legends of Catalonia beginning in 1890. The dragon had many names, including Guita Boja, La Guita Xica, Mulaguita, La Mulassa, Mula Fera, and Mula Guita. Its name transformed over time, originally started as Mulassa, then Mulaguita, and finally Guita by the twentieth century. The name La Mulassa comes from an older term, mulassas, meaning 'monstrous mules,' which was used in Catalan mythology to refer to mule-dragon hybrids. La Guita Xica was originally considered a demon, but has become a protective spirit over the past century. It is also called a tarasca, which is a name for draconic creatures of Spanish and Latin American folklore. La Guita Xica was half-mule and half-dragon. This comes from Catalan mountains where the mule remains a richly evocative animal. It had a strong practical importance, but it is also known for its temperament, which was disruptive and uneasy to the point where its domestication was considered untrustworthy. Originally La Guita Xica was considered a threatening force but it is now considered a protective dragon that defends the people of Catalonia and the Eucharist's festivals of Patum de Berga. During the festivals, large representations of the dragon are built in the town squares, spitting fireworks. It has a green body similar to that of an equine, and a very long neck and fangs. La Guita Xica's neck has been likened to that of the Loch Ness Monster.

description.en: Lai Khutshangbi (/laai-khoot-shaang-bee/) is a demoness (hingchabi) in Meitei mythology and folklore of Antique Kangleipak (Ancient Manipur). She has very long hands. The word "Lai" means "deity or divinity," "Khut" means "hand," and "Sangbi" or "Shangbi" means "long" in Manipuri (Meitei). The legend says that when she walks, her long hands touch the ground. Her fingers are as sharp as thorns. She has a large mouth with a long tongue. Her appearance is very frightening.

description.en: The leannán sídhe (Irish: [ˈl̠ʲan̪ˠaːnˠ ˈʃiː]; lit. 'fairy lover'; Scottish Gaelic: leannan sìth, Manx: lhiannan shee) is a figure from Celtic mythology. She is depicted as a beautiful woman of the Aos Sí ("people of the fairy mounds") who takes a human lover. Lovers of the leannán sídhe are said to live brief, though highly inspired, lives. The name comes from the Gaelic words for a sweetheart or lover and the term for inhabitants of fairy mounds (fairy). While the leannán sídhe is most often depicted as a female fairy, there is at least one reference to a male leannán sídhe troubling a mortal woman. A version of the myth was popularized during the Celtic Revival in the late 19th-century. The leannán sídhe is mentioned by Jane Wilde, writing as "Speranza", in her 1887 Ancient Legends, Mystic Charms and Superstitions of Ireland. W. B. Yeats popularized his own 'newly-ancient' version of the leannán sídhe, emphasizing the spirit's almost vampiric tendencies. As he imagined it, the leannán sídhe is depicted as a beautiful muse who offers inspiration to an artist in exchange for their love and devotion; although the supernatural affair leads to madness and eventual death for the artist: The Leanhaun Shee (fairy mistress) seeks the love of mortals. If they refuse, she must be their slave; if they consent, they are hers, and can only escape by finding another to take their place. The fairy lives on their life, and they waste away. Death is no escape from her. She is the Gaelic muse, for she gives inspiration to those she persecutes. The Gaelic poets die young, for she is restless, and will not let them remain long on earth—this malignant phantom.

description.id: Leprechaun (bahasa Irlandia: leipreachán) dalam mitologi Irlandia adalah sebangsa peri jantan yang mendiami daratan Irlandia. Bersama peri-peri lainnya, Leprechaun mendiami daratan Irlandia sebelum kedatangan bangsa Kelt. Mereka digambarkan sebagai lelaki tua yang senang berbuat nakal. Mereka berdagang dengan menjual batu kerikil atau menjadi pembuat sepatu. Mereka dikatakan sangat kaya. Menurut legenda, leprechaun memiliki sebuah gentong yang berisi emas. Gentong tersebut dikatakan di letakkan di ujung pelangi. Dikatakan bahwa siapapun yang berhasil mencuri gentong emas tersebut, maka sang dewa muslihat tersebut harus mengabulkan 3 permintaan jika gentongnya ingin dikembalikan. Pada saat perayaan Hari Hijau atau hari untuk mengingat Santo Patrick, dikatakan leprechaun akan datang kerumah seseorang. Karena itu disetiap negara saat merayakan hari ini anak-anak mulai berlomba-lomba untuk menangkap leprechaun. Cerita rakyat tentang leprechaun ini berasal dari Irlandia, mulai tersebar bersamaan dengan tersebarnya perayaan hari St. Patrick ke berbagai negara.
description.en: A leprechaun (Irish: lucharachán/leipreachán/luchorpán) is a diminutive supernatural being in Irish folklore, classed by some as a type of solitary fairy. They are usually depicted as little bearded men, wearing a coat and hat, who partake in mischief. In later times, they have been depicted as shoe-makers who have a hidden pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. Leprechaun-like creatures rarely appear in Irish mythology and only became prominent in later folklore.

description.en: Lí Ban or Liban (from Old Irish lí 'beauty' and ban 'of women', hence 'paragon of women'), in the legend surrounding the formation of Lough Neagh, was a woman turned mermaid who inhabited the area before the great lake gushed up on dry land. Her family was drowned, but she survived in an underwater chamber in the lake for a year, after which she was transformed into a being who was half-human, half-salmon. In her mermaid form, she was spotted by the ship carrying a messenger sent by St. Comgall to Rome. She promised to meet at the seaport inlet of Inbhear nOllarbha (Larne Lough) in Ireland after one year, and was captured in a fishnet. There she was baptised by Comgall, and given the Christened name Muirgein ("sea-born") or Muirgeilt ("sea-wander"). She appears as Saint Muirgen in genealogies of Irish saints with her feast day assigned to 27 January. The mermaid figure may ultimately derive from another Lí Ban, Sister of Fand, in Irish mythology.
